summary.text: 牛 depicts an ox’s head and horns and is used for the animal, including cattle. It also serves as a character radical.

formation.text: Pictographic: the graph depicts an ox’s head and horns. The cited analysis describes oracle-bone and bronze forms as frontal views; some bronze forms are said to show ears, eyes, and nose as well.

history.text: The transmitted Shuowen description refers to horns, head, and a tail or raised-back feature. Its gloss calls 牛 a large sacrificial animal; Duan Yucai later proposes a different interpretation based on the animal’s work and patterns. These are historical interpretations, not independent proof of the graph’s origin.

The recorded form classes include oracle-bone, bronze, Chu manuscript, and small-seal forms. The specimens are not individually dated in the supplied account, so this sequence does not establish the earliest surviving example or a dated path of graphic change.
牛 is reported for cattle and in personal names in bronze inscriptions, but the cited examples do not establish when either use began.

uncertainties.text: The head-and-horns pictographic analysis is supported. The earliest securely dated specimen and dates of the listed form classes remain unresolved; no competing formation or specific graphic corruption is documented in the inspected evidence.
A modern dictionary lists figurative stubbornness, star-name, zodiac, calendar, and surname uses. Their dates and connections to the animal sense are not established by the supplied evidence.

Supplied local data gives Mandarin niú and Baxter–Sagart Middle Chinese ngjuw and Old Chinese *[ŋ]ʷə. The character-specific Unihan record could not be accessed. These readings do not establish graphic formation, and 牛 is not analyzed as a phonetic component.

senses.text: The graph is interpreted as depicting the animal, and 牛 is reported in an inscription referring to cattle. The earliest securely dated occurrence is unresolved, so this is the earliest supported sense, not a dated first use.

senses.period: Shuowen Jiezi; date of use not established here
senses.text: The transmitted Shuowen entry glosses 牛 as a large sacrificial animal. This dictionary gloss does not establish a separate earlier sense or the graph’s original meaning.

limitations.text: No dated corpus of written senses establishes the chronology or semantic connections among the animal, figurative, astronomical, calendar, zodiac, and surname uses.

overview.text: 牛 depicts an ox’s head and horns and is used for the animal: ox or cattle.
